overview:
In Jain philosophy, the **Taijasa body (taijasa-śarīra)** is one of the four fundamental bodies (śarīras) that a soul may possess, described across both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. It is classified as a subtle, luminous, and energy‑based body composed of tejas (heat, radiance). Unlike the gross physical body (audārika) or the karmic body (kārmaṇa), the Taijasa body is not visible to the senses. It functions as the internal energetic mechanism that enables digestion, metabolism, bodily warmth, and the activation of sensory and mental processes.

Jain texts describe the Taijasa body as arising from **Taijasa vargaṇās**, extremely subtle aggregates of energy‑particles that the soul attracts and binds through its karmic dispositions. These vargaṇās form a body that accompanies the soul across rebirths, though its configuration changes according to karmic conditions. The Taijasa body is essential for the functioning of the physical body but is metaphysically distinct from it; it is also distinct from the fiery or radiant bodies of celestial beings, though related in its energetic nature.

In cosmological and karmic analysis, the Taijasa body plays a crucial role in explaining how the soul interacts with matter, how bodily processes occur, and how karmic influx (āsrava) and bondage (bandha) are mediated. It is also involved in the transition of the soul at death, helping separate the soul from the gross body and enabling the formation of the next embodiment. Advanced Jain metaphysics further connects the Taijasa body to the **Gunasthāna** progression, noting that its refinement parallels the reduction of passions and karmic density.

Across traditions, the Taijasa body is consistently treated as a subtle, indispensable component of embodied existence, bridging the gap between the soul’s consciousness and the physical processes of life.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: The Taijasa body is composed of energy (tejas).
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.38 lists the four bodies: audārika, vaikriya, āhāraka, and taijasa. Commentaries (Sarvārthasiddhi, Tattvārthavṛtti) explain the Taijasa body as the subtle heat‑body responsible for digestion and bodily warmth.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra Jīvakāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta Chakravartin
primary_sources.translation: The Taijasa body is an aggregate formed from Taijasa vargaṇās.
primary_sources.notes: This Digambara text provides detailed classifications of vargaṇās and explains how the Taijasa body accompanies the soul through saṃsāra.

primary_sources.title: Pañcāstikāya
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda
primary_sources.translation: The nature of the Taijasa body serves as a cause for bodily functioning.
primary_sources.notes: Kundakunda’s Prakrit exposition links the Taijasa body to the soul’s interaction with matter and the functioning of embodied life.

misconceptions.myth: The Taijasa body is the same as the physical heat generated by the human body.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts describe the Taijasa body as a subtle, non-physical energetic body composed of tejas vargaṇās. Physical heat is only one outward manifestation of its deeper metaphysical role.

misconceptions.myth: Only certain beings possess a Taijasa body.
misconceptions.reality: All embodied souls in saṃsāra possess a Taijasa body, regardless of realm or form. It is a universal component of embodied existence.

misconceptions.myth: The Taijasa body disappears at death.
misconceptions.reality: The Taijasa body separates from the gross body at death and accompanies the soul until the next embodiment, reforming according to karmic conditions.
